nameStory: Micrasterias torreyi is named after John Torrey, a pioneering 19th-century American botanist who helped catalog many of our continent's plants. The genus name 'Micrasterias' comes from Greek words meaning 'small star,' referring to the beautiful star-like shape of these microscopic algae when viewed under magnification.
description: Micrasterias torreyi is actually not a plant at all, but a single-celled green alga that lives in freshwater ponds and lakes. This tiny organism is invisible to the naked eye, measuring only about 0.1 millimeters across, but under a microscope it reveals an intricate, symmetrical star-shaped form with elegant lobes and projections. Like other green algae, it contains chlorophyll and makes its own food through photosynthesis, contributing to the green tint you might notice in some pond water. Each cell is essentially a living work of art, with two mirror-image halves joined at the center.

idTips.label: Star-shaped symmetry
idTips.description: Under magnification, the cell shows perfect bilateral symmetry with elaborate lobes extending outward like points of a decorative star

idTips.label: Constricted center
idTips.description: The cell pinches inward at the middle where the two halves meet, creating a distinctive waist-like appearance

idTips.label: Green coloration
idTips.description: The cell appears bright green due to chloroplasts distributed throughout, giving it a jewel-like appearance under proper lighting

idTips.label: Size range
idTips.description: Cells measure roughly 100-150 micrometers across, about the thickness of a human hair

idTips.label: Smooth cell wall
idTips.description: The outer edge appears relatively smooth without the spines or projections found on some related species

habitat: This microscopic alga inhabits quiet freshwater environments like ponds, small lakes, and slow-moving streams throughout New England, particularly in areas with soft, slightly acidic water. You'll find it most commonly in woodland ponds and bog environments where the water is naturally stained with tannins from decomposing leaves. It prefers nutrient-poor waters and is often associated with sphagnum moss and other bog plants.

seasonality.spring: Populations begin growing as water temperatures warm and daylight increases, though you'd need a microscope to observe them.
seasonality.summer: Peak abundance occurs during warm months when the algae reproduce most actively through cell division.
seasonality.fall: Numbers may decline as temperatures drop, but some individuals persist in deeper water layers.
seasonality.winter: Dormant stages survive freezing temperatures, ready to resume growth when conditions improve.

funFact: Despite being a single cell with no brain or nervous system, Micrasterias can actually 'see' light and will slowly move toward it by changing the distribution of weight within its cell body - essentially doing microscopic yoga to follow the sun!
confusionNotes: Under the microscope, it might be confused with other star-shaped desmids like Micrasterias radiosa, but M. torreyi typically has more rounded, less deeply cut lobes and lacks the intricate secondary divisions found in some relatives.
contextualKnowledge: Though called 'algae,' these organisms are more closely related to land plants than to seaweeds, representing an ancient lineage that helped give rise to all terrestrial plant life. Finding them requires specialized equipment, so citizen science pond surveys often focus on larger, visible aquatic life instead.
compareHints: Compared to other Micrasterias species in New England waters, M. torreyi tends to have simpler, less ornate lobing patterns than the deeply dissected M. pinnatifida or the heavily spined M. radiosa. Its relatively smooth outline and moderate size help distinguish it from both the more elaborate and the more simplified species in this diverse genus.
